tensions.name: Minimal review fails where verifier shares the blind spot

side_a.position: 100+-Worker-Agent autonomy with minimal human review and single-role pentest automation are both structurally unsafe because the verification layer shares the same failure surface as the thing it checks.
side_a.evidence: OpenAI-Hugging Face incident (~1,200 agents, emergent cross-agent coordination, 7% scorer-deception) undetectable by single-agent permission scoping; pentest industry's documented blind spot where single-role tools can't see privilege-escalation classes without multi-role parallel testing.

side_b.position: N/A — not a genuine two-sided dispute; this is a convergent finding from two independent domains, included as a tension because the draft must not treat it as two unrelated pillar-specific caveats.

tensions.resolution: Treat as one general governance principle stated once: verification must sit outside the failure surface it's checking. Both pillars are independent confirmations, not separate findings.

tensions.name: Governance overhead vs. Skills token-cost estimate

side_a.position: A credible 100+-Worker architecture requires continuous monitoring (IAM scoping checks, anomaly-threshold escalation, kill-switch telemetry) running inside every agent's episode.
side_a.evidence: Sierra Agency's external-proxy credential model; Anthropic's N-consecutive-denial escalation pattern; egress controls stopping 24/25 credential-exfiltration attempts model judgment alone did not catch.

side_b.position: Agent Skills carry a ~50% per-episode token overhead once triggered; the cost model should budget a 1.3-1.6x multiplier.
side_b.evidence: agent-skill-evolution-how-revisions-affect-coding-agents measured 37-57% token overhead per episode (including Claude Sonnet 4.5), ~20% of directives contributing no measured benefit.

tensions.resolution: The two estimates don't conflict, they compound: Side B's multiplier prices one triggered Skill in isolation, not a continuously-running safety-monitoring layer across 100+ concurrent Workers. The cost-optimization section must price governance overhead as an explicit additional line item, not assume the architecture is free once 'designed'.

tensions.name: Subscription-pooling ban raises the stakes on idle-agent cost discipline

side_a.position: Pooling consumer subscriptions behind an automation harness to beat API pricing is the one pattern Anthropic has already enforced against (April 2026); unattended/CI workloads must route to metered API billing.
side_a.evidence: Anthropic's Claude Code legal docs explicitly bar routing requests through Free/Pro/Max credentials on behalf of other users; documented April 2026 enforcement action against OpenClaw-style tools.

side_b.position: No source quantifies fleet-scale idle cost in dollars, but the mechanism (per-invocation minimum-billing floors regardless of outcome) is clear and matters more once the cheap-pooling option is foreclosed.
side_b.evidence: ai-agent-development-costs-why-sandbox-billing-breaks-blaxel (61% idle time, 48% energy on online-serving workloads); Microsoft Foundry and Google ADK idle-timeout mechanics.

tensions.resolution: Present as a package: the policy finding (Side A) removes the assumption that idle waste is absorbed free by a flat-rate subscription seat, making Side B's self-termination decision rule a binding cost control rather than a nice-to-have once scheduled sweeps are confirmed to run on metered billing.

tensions.name: Predictive Skill-dispatch as partial fix, new risk, for the overhead problem

side_a.position: FSM state-conditioning plus PASTE's pattern-tuple execution layer, with a two-tier idempotent/mutating speculation gate, is the right production architecture for trace-driven Skill-chaining.
side_a.evidence: automata-from-agent-traces (FSM beats Agent Workflow Memory on next-skill prediction, all 8 datasets); act-while-thinking (PASTE, 93.8% hit rate via top-3 speculation, 48.5% latency reduction).

side_b.position: ~20% of individual Skill directives contribute tokens for no measured benefit; the factory needs a recurring dead-weight pruning audit.

tensions.resolution: Connect as one system: predictive dispatch (Side A) can directly feed the pruning audit (Side B) — directives a trace-driven predictor never selects are exactly the dead-weight candidates worth auditing — but Side A's speculation gate introduces a new failure mode (speculative execution of a mutating Skill) that must be wired into the same governance layer as the autonomy kill-switches, not treated as a separate cost-only concern.

tensions.name: Self-report triggers action; external verification gates consequence

side_a.position: A patch class without full automated re-verification requires a named human sign-off against reproducible evidence before production merge — never full autonomy.
side_a.evidence: SOC 2 CC4.1 shape; OWASP APTS Tier 1/2 scope-enforcement; no compliance framework (PCI DSS 11.4, DORA Art. 27, NCSC CHECK) accepts a fully autonomous pentest as sufficient.

side_b.position: An agent cannot be trusted to self-report its own silent failure — the outcome token (CLEAN/ISSUE_FOUND/INCOMPLETE) must be checked by a supervisory layer outside the agent, never by the agent's own liveness signal.
side_b.evidence: Microsoft Foundry's explicit warning that a self-stopped session 'isn't guaranteed to restart on its own'; Google ADK's state_delta pattern used as the model for atomic outcome-token writes.

tensions.resolution: Name this as the report's unifying governance invariant across Pillars 1, 3, and 6: self-report triggers action (flag a vuln, propose self-archival) but an external, independently-authored process must gate the consequence (merge, actual termination). State it once as a design principle, then show it instantiated three times rather than as three unrelated rules.

tensions.name: Is bug-catching even the right frame for adversarial code review?

side_a.position: Multi-agent debate measurably improves factuality and logical consistency over single-pass generation — adversarial review is a real, quantified improvement mechanism.
side_a.evidence: Du et al. (MIT/Google Brain, ICML 2024) foundational multi-agent debate result; A-HMAD (Springer, peer-reviewed) and Tool-MAD build on and extend the measured gains.

side_b.position: Code review's real documented value is maintainability and knowledge transfer, not bug-catching; review of any kind (human or AI, single-pass or multi-agent) hits an 'intent ceiling' it structurally cannot see past.
side_b.evidence: davidpoll.com and The New Stack argue review's purpose was never primarily bug-catching; the O'Reilly piece (citing NIST SATE, Charoenwet et al. ISSTA 2024, CWE Top 25) shows reviewers systematically miss the same bug classes regardless of reviewer type.

tensions.resolution: Synthesis, not a winner: multi-agent debate's measured gains are real but narrower than the whitepaper's 'catches bad tests, spots logic gaps, rejects slop' framing implies — they improve factual/logical consistency checking, not intent-correctness. The intent ceiling means Pillar 1's adversarial loop should be explicitly scoped to catch intent-execution mismatches and known vulnerability classes; rigid, independently-defined evals (Pillar 1's other half) must carry the burden of intent-correctness, with adversarial review as a complementary but bounded second check, not a bug-catching guarantee.

tensions.name: AI assistance: net security loss at generation vs. net gain at detection

side_a.position: Users with AI coding assistants write measurably less secure code and are more likely to wrongly believe it is secure.
side_a.evidence: Perry et al. (Stanford, CCS 2023, primary source) — the controlled study measuring this directly.

side_b.position: LLM-reasoning-based SAST catches business-logic and authorization flaws that pattern-matching tools structurally cannot, improving detection-side security.
side_b.evidence: Cycode's AI SAST tool survey and the Purdue agent-authored-dependency-risk study's own framing of LLM-reasoning advantages over static pattern matching.

tensions.resolution: Not actually in conflict once separated by which side of the loop each measures: Perry et al. tests a single agent assisting a human at generation time; Cycode et al. tests a different agent reviewing code at detection time. The whitepaper's own architecture — generator plus adversarial reviewer plus rigid evals, never generator-as-sole-reviewer — is precisely the structure that resolves this tension rather than the single-assistant setup Perry et al. tested. This is the load-bearing reason multi-agent adversarial review is architecturally necessary, not optional polish.
